rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient at moderate temperature to capture all 10 compounds, reveal the overall elution window, and reduce risk of truncation while still showing where critical pairs sit.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so optimize time by trimming the gradient to the observed elution window and shortening it. The first run suggests the peaks elute roughly between phi about 0.11 and 0.40, so this should keep all compounds in-gradient while pulling the last peak earlier.

Resolution is still comfortably above threshold, so the next move is to shorten the gradient further while keeping the same window and temperature. This directly tests how much time can be saved before the critical mid-cluster pair begins to lose too much resolution.

The current method is at the score ceiling but only just meets the 10 min target, so the best remaining opportunity is to compress time one more step. This probes whether the limiting pair can still stay at or above R=1.5 while moving the last peak safely under 10 min.

The 6 min gradient was too steep for the critical pair, so keep the successful 8 min window but raise temperature to pull the last peak below 10 min. Temperature may slightly alter selectivity, so this is the cleanest way to seek a more robust perfect-score method.

Temperature worsened the critical pair, so return to 40 C and instead make the gradient window slightly lower and narrower. That should keep the problematic mid-cluster pair in a shallower local slope while still covering the observed elution range and may pull the last peak just under 10 min.

Lowering the window increased retention too much, so test a slightly higher phi1 at the successful 8 min, 40 C conditions to pull the last peak below 10 min while perturbing selectivity less drastically than changing temperature. This is a direct refinement around the current best method.

The critical pair is highly temperature-sensitive and worsened at 45 C, so test a lower temperature from the proven 8 min, 0.15–0.55 window. This may improve the 6/7 selectivity while keeping the last peak near 10 min, potentially yielding a more robust perfect-score condition.

Bracket around the best condition by slightly lowering phi1 from 0.55 to 0.50 at 40 C. This should reduce gradient steepness enough to strengthen the marginal 6/7 separation while testing whether the last peak can still remain at or below 10 min.

Shift the same 8 min window slightly upward by raising phi0 while keeping phi1 fixed. This should move the whole chromatogram earlier and may keep the last peak under 10 min without increasing the local slope around the critical 6/7 pair as much as raising phi1 did.

The current best is perfect but still has margin to test a slightly stronger start, which may shorten the run further. This probes whether the critical 6/7 pair stays at or above R=1.5 while improving speed beyond the new optimum.

The new best method has only a tiny margin on the 6/7 pair, so shortening tG at the same window is the key boundary test. If this still resolves 6/7 at R>=1.5, it would give a faster perfect-score method; if not, injection 10 is confirmed as near-optimal.

From the 0.20–0.55, 8 min optimum, slightly lowering phi1 should shallow the gradient and improve the marginal 6/7 separation while keeping retention lower than the 0.15–0.50 case. This checks whether a narrower, shifted-up window can retain a perfect score with a bit more robustness.

Explore whether a broader, slightly longer upper-shifted window can keep the sensitive 6/7 pair fully resolved while perhaps moving the last compound earlier through a higher final strength. This is a useful bracket around the best method to see if there is another robust CRF-1.000 region.

The 0.20–0.60 window preserved full resolution at 10 min, so shorten it to 8 min to see whether it can also reach the score ceiling. This directly tests whether a higher-phi1 window can match or beat the current best while keeping all pairs resolved.

Now test whether the best 0.20–0.55 window has extra resolution headroom at a slightly longer gradient. If it does, that confirms injection 10 is the shortest member of a robust perfect-score plateau and helps define the safe operating space around the optimum.

We have mapped the 0.20-start region well except for the fast extreme at higher phi1, so this tests the shortest high-strength variant. It should show whether phi1 0.60 can compensate enough for a 6 min gradient to preserve the critical 6/7 pair while giving the fastest run in this neighborhood.

The data show a clear tradeoff: higher phi1 speeds the run but erodes the 6/7 pair. Testing phi1 0.65 at the otherwise optimal 0.20, 8 min, 40 C point extends that trend and confirms whether the best condition truly sits near phi1 0.55.

At this point the best score is already achieved, so use remaining budget to probe selectivity around the optimum. A lower temperature at the best window will show whether the critical 6/7 pair can gain resolution margin without introducing a severe time penalty or a new weak pair.

Temperature clearly changes selectivity in this mixture, and we have not yet checked the high-temperature side from the current best window. A 50 C run will complete that map and confirm whether 40 C is truly the unique optimum around the best gradient conditions.

A final low-temperature check completes the temperature profile at the best gradient window. The strong selectivity changes already seen suggest 40 C may be a narrow sweet spot, and this run will verify the edge behavior rather than risk repeating similar gradient conditions.

Complete the temperature map at the best gradient by checking the hottest allowed condition. Since both lower and moderately higher temperatures degraded resolution, this final edge test will confirm how sharply centered the optimum is around 40 C.

Use one of the remaining injections to test whether the higher-temperature loss of 6/7 resolution can be offset by shifting back to the lower 0.15 start. This explores a different selectivity/speed balance than the current best while staying close to proven fully eluting conditions.

With the optimum already found, use the penultimate injection to test the nearby condition that should maximize resolution headroom while staying close to the time threshold. This helps define a robust backup method near the best region in case more margin on the critical pair is desired.

The optimum is already known, so use the last injection to probe the only untested adjacent temperature to the best method. This will confirm whether 40 C is a sharp optimum or whether a small temperature increase preserves full resolution at the same fast gradient.
